topics.title: Dr Sadao's house by the sea

learn.hook: War between Japan and America. A Japanese surgeon trained in America. One misty evening, the war washes up on his beach.
points: Author: Pearl S. Buck, an American writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.
Setting: Japan during the Second World War, when Japan and the USA were enemies.
Dr Sadao Hoki, a skilled Japanese surgeon trained in America, lives in a house on the Japanese coast with his wife Hana.
His father had valued education and Japan's future. Sadao met Hana in America, and they married in Japan with their families' approval.

example.q: Why is it significant that Sadao was trained in America?
steps: He learnt his surgical skill in America.
Japan and America are now at war.
So he owes his skill to the country of the 'enemy'.
example.answer: He owes his medical skill to America, the enemy nation, which deepens the dilemma he will face.

learn.reallife: Many Indian doctors train abroad and serve at home, at AIIMS or district hospitals. Medicine crosses borders even when politics divides them.

topics.title: A wounded enemy on the shore

learn.hook: Through the mist, Sadao and Hana see a body on the rocks. The cap says 'U.S. Navy'. What would you do?
points: In the evening mist, Sadao and Hana find a wounded white man washed up on the shore; his cap reads 'U.S. Navy'.
He is an escaped American prisoner of war with a gunshot wound.
Sadao and Hana are torn between patriotism (hand him over) and humanity (save his life). They take him into their house.
The servants disapprove and refuse to help; later they leave the house together.

example.q: Why are Sadao and Hana torn about what to do?
steps: As patriots, they should hand over an enemy.
As human beings, and Sadao as a doctor, they should save a dying man.
Helping him also puts them at risk.
example.answer: Their duty to their country clashes with their humanity and Sadao's medical duty, and helping him is dangerous.

learn.reallife: Doctors in conflict zones, like those with the International Committee of the Red Cross, are trained to treat every wounded person, friend or foe.

learn.hook: Sadao removes the bullet, then confesses everything to the General, who promises to have the man quietly killed. Then he forgets.
points: Sadao operates and removes the bullet; Hana, after the maid Yumi refuses, washes the man and later feeds him herself.
Sadao is called to treat the ailing General and confesses that he is hiding the American.
The General promises to send his private assassins to kill the man silently and remove the body, so Sadao would not be blamed.
But the General forgets, absorbed in his own health; he needs Sadao for his own operation.

steps: He was ill and worried about his own operation.
He was self-centred and absorbed in his health.
So the matter of the American slipped from his mind.
example.answer: He was so absorbed in his own illness and needs that he forgot about the American.

learn.reallife: Hospitals in India follow strict medical ethics: a doctor's first duty is the patient's life. Sadao follows that rule even in war.

topics.title: A boat, a flashlight and an escape

learn.hook: No assassins arrive. Sadao makes his own plan: a boat, food, water and a flashlight.
points: When no assassins come, Sadao helps the American escape by boat to a nearby island, with food, water, clothes and a flashlight for signalling if he needs help.
The American gets away safely. Sadao wonders why he could not simply kill him.
This is how Sadao finally solves his problem: he follows his conscience as a doctor and a human being, while protecting his family from discovery.

example.q: How did Sadao finally solve his problem?
steps: The General's plan failed, so the man was still there.
Sadao could not kill a patient he had saved.
He arranged a boat, food and a flashlight so the American could escape.
example.answer: He helped the American escape secretly by boat, saving both the man's life and his own family from trouble.

learn.reallife: The Geneva Conventions protect wounded soldiers and prisoners of war. Sadao's choice reflects that spirit even when people around him want the enemy dead.

topics.title: Sadao, Hana, the General and the title's irony

learn.hook: Who is 'the enemy'? The wounded American, the self-centred General, or hatred itself?
points: Dr Sadao: a dedicated surgeon torn between nationalism and humanity; his professional ethics win.
Hana: compassionate and supportive; she washes and feeds the enemy herself when the servants refuse.
The General: self-centred and pragmatic; he offers murder and then forgets because of his own health.
Devices: third-person narration; irony (the General forgets); the title's irony about who 'the enemy' really is.

example.q: Explain the irony of the title 'The Enemy'.
steps: The American is officially the enemy.
Yet Sadao and Hana treat him with humanity.
The real enemy may be hatred, prejudice and war itself.
example.answer: The 'enemy' by nationality is saved by kindness, suggesting the true enemy is hatred and war, not a person.

learn.reallife: In real life too, labels like 'enemy' often fade when one human being faces another in need.

topics.title: Themes: humanity, medical ethics and compassion in war

learn.hook: A doctor's oath does not ask for a passport. Sadao proves it in the middle of a war.
points: Humanity above patriotism and prejudice: Sadao and Hana save a man whom their country calls the enemy.
Professional ethics: a doctor's first duty is to save life; Sadao cannot let a patient die.
Hatred in war versus individual compassion: the servants and the General reflect wartime hatred; Sadao and Hana show personal kindness.

example.q: How do professional ethics guide Sadao?
steps: As a surgeon, his duty is to save life.
He operates on the American even though it is risky.
He cannot kill the man he has healed.
example.answer: His duty as a doctor to save life outweighs national hatred; he heals the man and later helps him escape.

learn.reallife: Under the Geneva Conventions, medical teams in war must care for all wounded people without discrimination, the very principle Sadao follows.

learn.hook: 'Sadao's dilemma' is the classic long answer from Vistas. Know its two sides, and the marks follow.
points: Sadao's dilemma: duty to his country (hand over the enemy) versus duty as a doctor (save a dying man).
Why the servants left: they believed sheltering an enemy was wrong and dangerous. The General: self-centred, cares only for his own health.
Short answers on Sadao (dedicated, ethical, torn) and Hana (compassionate, supportive).
Long answer on humanity versus patriotism: the discovery, the operation, the General's failed plan, the escape, and the message.

example.q: Write a 50-word answer: What was Sadao's dilemma?
steps: As a patriot, he should hand over an enemy prisoner.
As a doctor, he must save the dying man.
Helping him risked his family's safety.
example.answer: Sadao had to choose between patriotism and humanity. As a loyal Japanese he should hand over the escaped American prisoner, but as a doctor he could not let a wounded man die. Helping him also endangered his family.

learn.reallife: Films and stories often show soldiers or doctors helping a wounded rival. The board exam often asks students to connect such ideas to 'The Enemy'.
